title: Empty Hands, Not Full Ones
teaser: Receiving the gospel is not assenting to a list of beliefs. It is trust — that the work has already been done. Empty hands, not full ones.
theme: Faith is the posture of empty hands toward a finished work.
framework: Chiastic application — what receiving the news of Day 3 actually looks like in a body, in a week, in a life that has tried hard and grown tired.

emphasis: I am not ashamed of the gospel
the power of God for salvation
The righteous will live by faith
modules.passage: I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, first to the Jew, then to the Greek. For the gospel reveals the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish, just as it is written: 'The righteous will live by faith.'

modules.heading: A Word You Have Inherited Without Choosing
modules.body:
Most people who use the word faith have inherited a definition they would not actually defend if you asked them to defend it.

In ordinary English, faith now tends to mean something like a private inner conviction held without enough evidence to call it knowledge. A leap. A bet. A feeling about something invisible.

If that is what faith means, receiving the gospel sounds like an exercise in working yourself up to a state of belief. You read the four lines from yesterday. You decide whether you can convince yourself they are true. The whole thing becomes a small interior performance — a quiet, lonely persuasion of the self by the self.

This is, in fact, what a lot of people who have walked away from Christianity remember being asked to do. To believe harder. To stop having questions. To square away their doubts before approaching the person at the center. Plenty of readers come to this page with a long history of trying that, and a small ache where the trying used to live.

Welcome back to Day 4.

The news of yesterday — that the message is a person, that the announcement is what He did and what was done to Him — leaves us with a question. If the message is a person, what does it mean to receive Him?

The word the New Testament uses, the word that gets translated faith in nearly every English Bible, is the Greek word pistis. It is the word Paul uses in Romans 1:16 and 17. It does not mean what modern English faith means. It means something older, and stranger, and much more freeing.

We will look at that word. We will follow it back to its Hebrew cousin. Then we will follow it forward, into a sentence Martin Luther wrote when he could not sleep — a sentence that started a fire that has not gone out yet.

The ground of today is small. Whatever you have been told you had to do to be acceptable, the four lines from yesterday say it has already been done. The climbing is not what is being asked of you.

What is being asked is harder, and easier, than the climb.

modules.definition: Trust, allegiance, fidelity. Often translated 'faith' in English.
modules.rootMeaning: From the verb peithō (πείθω), 'to persuade, to be convinced.' But the noun travels well past private conviction. Pistis names a relational bond — the kind of trust that puts weight on another person.
modules.usage: In the Greek-speaking Roman world Paul wrote in, pistis was a public-square word as well as a private one. It named the loyalty between a soldier and his commander, the fidelity between a client and his patron, the bond holding a marriage together. To say someone had pistis toward another person did not mean they had a feeling about that person. It meant their life was bent in that direction — that they had thrown their weight on that person and were walking forward as though the person could be relied on.
modules.usageNote: In the Septuagint — the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible done about 250 BC — the translators chose pistis to render the Hebrew word emunah (אֱמוּנָה, Strong's H530). Emunah comes from a root meaning 'to support, to be firm, to carry.' It is the same root behind the word amen. Habakkuk 2:4 uses it: 'the just shall live by his faith' — by his emunah, by his faithful response. When Paul quotes that verse in Romans 1:17 with the Greek pistis, he collapses centuries of Hebrew meaning into one Greek word. The muscle of the original is trust as a posture of the whole life, not belief as a private conviction.

relatedWords.note: Hebrew counterpart, from a root meaning 'to support, to carry.' The word behind 'amen' — and the word Paul translates with pistis when he quotes Habakkuk in Romans 1:17.
the verb form — 'to trust, to rely on.' Used 243 times in the New Testament; nearly always points at a person, not a proposition.

modules.heading: The Sentence That Broke Luther Open
modules.body:
Romans 1:17 is a single sentence, and it once broke a man.

The man was Martin Luther. By the time he tried to read the verse honestly, he was a thirty-something Augustinian monk in Wittenberg, a doctor of theology lecturing on Paul's letter, and — by his own later testimony — a person in chronic spiritual agony. Luther was not a slacker. He fasted to the point of damaging his health. He confessed his sins for hours, then went back into the confessional an hour later because he had remembered another one. He ground at the practice of his religion the way a person grinds at a wound. And the phrase in Romans 1:17 that mentioned 'the righteousness of God' had become the exact place where the wound was.

He assumed — as nearly every reader before him had — that 'the righteousness of God' meant the standard of moral perfection God demands. Read that way, the gospel is not good news. It is a publication of the standard against which the human being is going to be measured and found wanting. Luther read the verse and felt only the standard. He felt, in his words from the autobiographical preface to his 1545 Latin works, that he hated this God who demanded what no one could deliver.

Then, sometime in the late 1510s, the verse cracked open for him.

'The righteousness of God' is not the righteousness God demands. It is the righteousness God gives. The phrase is not describing a moral bar that has to be cleared. It is describing a gift that has already been handed across the table, paid for in advance, and laid in front of the human being who has neither earned it nor been able to earn it. The genitive 'of God' is, on this reading, possessive rather than evaluative — the righteousness that comes from God, not the righteousness demanded against the human being from God's high court.

Read that way, the gospel is good news.

The Berean Standard Bible we are reading translates the verse 'the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish.' From the first instant of the gift to the last, the engine driving the whole exchange is not the human being's effort. It is the human being's trust. Faith from start to finish. Pistis from beginning to end.

Luther later wrote of that moment of reading: 'I felt myself reborn and to have entered through open gates into paradise itself.' It was not a feeling-conversion in the modern revivalist sense. It was a reading-conversion. A single sentence in a single epistle, read finally without the mistranslation his own anxiety had been laying on top of it, gave him back the gospel.

Four years later he nailed his ninety-five theses to the door of the Wittenberg church.

This matters for the reader because Luther was almost everything modern readers are not. He was inside the religious system from boyhood. He had every credential. He had memorized vast tracts of Scripture in Latin. He could quote the Fathers. He had done all the religion. And the religion had not given him the gospel. It took a sentence read honestly to give him the news.

If the religion has not given you the gospel either, you are not the first.

The word the Reformers later used to compress this whole reframing was sola fide — Latin for 'by faith alone.' The slogan can sound like a flag in a culture war, but the underlying claim is exact. If the work has already been done, the only fitting human response is to receive what was finished without us. Adding our own work to the gift does not strengthen the gift. It denies the gift was ever finished.

The righteousness in the verse is not a wall. It is a robe. The verb in the four-line creed is not 'do.' It is 'has been done.'

emphasis: the just shall live by his faith
modules.passage: Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith.

modules.ancientTruth: When Paul quoted 'the just shall live by his faith' in Romans 1:17, he was reaching back six hundred years to the prophet Habakkuk, who had used the Hebrew word emunah — a word from the root behind 'amen,' a word that means firmness, faithful response, trust that carries weight. The Greek translators of Habakkuk had rendered emunah with pistis, the public-square word for loyalty and allegiance. Paul knew both. He used both.
modules.modernApplication: The English word faith has had, since roughly the Enlightenment, a quiet downward drift. Read a popular dictionary today and you will find faith defined as 'belief without evidence' or 'a strongly held conviction.' The relational muscle of pistis and emunah has been filed off. What is left is interior, private, almost frail — a feeling rather than a footing.
modules.connection: When the modern reader sees faith on the page of a Bible, the modern reader hears 'try to make yourself believe this.' When Habakkuk wrote it, and when Paul wrote it, what they meant was closer to 'put your weight on this and walk.' Same word in three languages. Three different muscles.
modules.question: If faith were not 'belief without evidence' but 'putting your weight on a person who has shown himself trustworthy,' what would change about how you have approached the gospel?
modules.answer: Probably this: the question would shift from 'do I believe enough' to 'is the person at the center of this someone I can lean on, and what would it look like to lean.' The first question has no honest answer. The second one does.
modules.newTestamentEcho: The Greek verb form pisteuō, used 243 times in the New Testament, almost never points at a proposition. It points at a person. 'Whoever pisteuei in him' — whoever leans on him, whoever throws their weight on him — is how John 3:16 reads in its original muscle.

modules.title: The Architect Who Tried Everything First
modules.content:
There was a woman in Pittsburgh, an architect named Rachel, who tried for eleven years to be a good Christian and discovered the trying was the obstacle, not the doorway. The story is hers in outline, though details are slightly composited.

She came to faith at twenty-two, in a campus group at her engineering school. The conversion was real and full. She prayed the prayer. She read the Bible cover to cover in her first year, twice. She joined a serious church, then a small group, then a leadership team, then a women's ministry committee that met before work on Tuesdays.

For about three years it felt right.

Around year four, she noticed the verses she had memorized were beginning to feel like items on a checklist she had completed. She tried harder. She added a morning quiet time. She added a journal practice. She added a fast.

By year six she was, in her own description, exhausted in a way that did not respond to sleep. She could not say it out loud, because in the church culture she was inside, exhaustion was understood as a failure of devotion. The cure for not feeling close to God was always to do more. So she did more.

By year nine she stopped going. Not in a crisis. Quietly. The journals stopped. The verses she had memorized began to feel like words from a foreign language she had once almost learned.

At year eleven, in the middle of an ordinary Tuesday in February, she was sitting on the floor of her apartment looking at a stack of devotional books on the coffee table. She had bought another one that week. It was still in its plastic wrap. She remembers thinking, very clearly: 'I cannot read another book that is going to ask me to do another thing.'

What she did next was ordinary. She did not go to church. She did not pray a prayer. She walked across the room and picked up the New Testament her grandmother had given her at her confirmation, the one she had not opened in nine years. She turned to Romans, more or less at random, and read for about ten minutes.

She got to chapter one, verse seventeen. She read the words 'the righteousness of God that comes by faith from start to finish.' She read them again. And she sat very still for a long time.

What had broken open in her was small and absolute. For eleven years she had thought the Christian life meant supplying her own righteousness — through quiet times, fasts, journaling, ministry, the whole apparatus of evangelical seriousness. The verse said the righteousness was already there. Already given. From start to finish. She had been trying to manufacture what had been laid in front of her on day one.

She sat on the floor and cried for a while, and then she put the book down. She did not run back to church. She did not start a new spiritual program. She started reading the New Testament again, slowly, the way a person reads letters from a friend rather than a textbook. The practices fell away one by one, until what was left was only what she actually wanted. She walked, in her phrase, 'with empty hands' for the first time since she had been twenty-two.

She has been a Christian, in the way Paul means the word, for fourteen years now. The first eleven, she would say, she had been climbing a ladder no one had asked her to climb. The last fourteen, she has been receiving a gift she had stopped trying to deserve.
modules.source: Composite narrative drawn from a pattern common among ex-evangelical and deconstructing readers. Names, locations, and identifying details adjusted; the sequence of events tracks several real testimonies.
modules.connection: Rachel's eleven years of climbing are what the law-shaped religious life looks like. Her quiet Tuesday on the floor, with the verse breaking the climbing open, is what reception of the gospel actually looks like. The trying was not the doorway. The trying was the wall.

modules.heading: The Letter Luther Wrote From Wartburg
modules.body:
On the first of August, 1521, Martin Luther sat at a desk in a tower of Wartburg Castle and wrote a letter to a young friend named Philip Melanchthon.

Luther was thirty-seven and in hiding. The Diet of Worms had ended a few months earlier. The Holy Roman Emperor had declared him an outlaw; the pope had excommunicated him; his prince had spirited him away to Wartburg under a false name to keep him alive. He was growing a beard and calling himself Junker Jörg, finishing the German New Testament that would change the language his country read its Bible in for centuries.

Melanchthon was twenty-four — the gentlest theological mind in Europe, a Greek scholar, a humanist. He was also, and Luther knew this, emotionally fragile. His letters in this period are full of scrupulous self-examination. He was tying himself in knots over his own sin. He was afraid he was not really converted. He was afraid that any wrong move would forfeit grace. The reformer of Wittenberg had a nervous breakdown coming if someone did not intervene.

Luther wrote him a letter. The relevant sentence runs:

'God does not save those who are only imaginary sinners. Be a sinner, and let your sins be strong, but let your trust in Christ be stronger.'

It is a startling sentence to read in isolation. It can sound, to a casual modern ear, like a permission slip for bad behavior. It is exactly the opposite. Slow down on this paragraph or miss what Luther is doing.

Luther is writing to a young man being eaten alive by his own scruples. Melanchthon is trying to be acceptable — trying to confess thoroughly enough, trying to repent purely enough, trying to cleanse his motives until they are unmixed enough that grace can safely apply to them. Luther's diagnosis is precise. The young man is treating sin as a thing to be made smaller, more manageable, more 'imaginary,' so he can present it for forgiveness in a state of presentable diminution. He is doing what Luther himself had spent fifteen years doing in the cloister. He is trying to be acceptable before approaching the throne.

Luther says: stop.

God, Luther writes, does not save imaginary sinners. He saves real ones. The economy of grace is not about scaling your sin down to the size your pride can carry. It is about bringing the whole, real, undiminished thing to Christ and trusting Him with it. The strength your soul needs in the moment of approach is not the strength to clean yourself up first. It is the strength of your trust in the one already cleaning you.

The sentence is the deepest possible cut against antinomianism. Antinomianism says sin doesn't matter because grace is here. Luther is saying sin matters terribly, and that is precisely why you cannot present a tidied-up version of it for inspection. You have to bring the actual one. And the strength to do that — the strength to come honestly, the strength to come empty-handed — is the strength of trust in someone whose work is finished.

This is the structural claim of the Reformation. Sola fide is not 'try to believe hard enough that the doctrine kicks in.' Sola fide — by faith alone — is 'come empty-handed because the work was finished without you, and there is nothing left to add.' The hand that has been clenched in production cannot, at the same moment, be open to receive. Either the work is finished or it is not. If it is, only empty hands fit the moment.

For the reader who has been told for years that her job was to perform until she became acceptable — who may, like Rachel from Pittsburgh, have done that performance for a decade and emptied out the bottom of her tank trying — Luther's letter is exactly the medicine. The bringing of the real, unsanitized self is not a failure of the spiritual life. It is the spiritual life. The cleaning up is not the precondition of the approach. It is the consequence of the approach. The hand opens, and only after it opens does the gift land in it.

Keep the verbs in order. The four-line creed of Day 3 said died, buried, raised, appeared. Past tense. Done. Romans 1:17 says 'comes by faith from start to finish.' Faith from start to finish. Not faith plus performance. Not faith later supplemented by works to make sure. Faith — pistis, emunah, trust — as the single posture that fits a finished work. Empty hands the whole way down.

This is also why the reader is not, at this point in the series, being asked to perform a decision. The series has not asked you to pray a sinner's prayer. It has not asked you to sign a doctrinal statement. The only thing the news asks of a person is to come honestly. The trust is not a thing you manufacture. It is a thing you discover already in your hand the moment you stop trying to fill the hand with something else.

If nothing else from this day stays with you, let it be this. The God Luther was writing about does not require imaginary sinners. He requires real ones — which is to say, He requires you, exactly as you are, with whatever set of failures and confusions and tired refusals you brought into this paragraph. The work was finished without you. The only question on the table is whether you will let your hands be empty enough to receive what was already laid down.

modules.title: Memorizing Romans 1:16
modules.prompt:
There is a long tradition, older than the printing press, of carrying a single sentence of scripture in the body so it is available without the book. Today we will learn one verse: Romans 1:16.

'I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes.'

The technique is called chunking. The mind does not memorize long strings well. It memorizes short phrases joined together. Break the verse into five short pieces and learn them one at a time:

  1. 'I am not ashamed'
  2. 'of the gospel'
  3. 'because it is the power of God'
  4. 'for salvation'
  5. 'to everyone who believes'

Say piece 1 out loud, three times, slowly. Then piece 2, three times. Now say pieces 1 and 2 together. Then piece 3, three times. Now pieces 1, 2, and 3 together. Continue until all five chunks join into the full verse.

If you stumble, do not start over from the top. Go back to the last chunk you said cleanly and rebuild from there. The verse will arrive in your mouth in two or three minutes.

Walk somewhere — to the kitchen, to a window, around the room. Say the verse out loud while walking. The body learns differently than the eye. A verse that has been spoken while moving lodges in a different drawer of the mind than one read silently.

Say it once before you sleep. Say it once when you wake. By tomorrow it will be in you, available without the book, the way a song you used to know is in you.
modules.follow_up: If memorizing scripture has religious baggage for you — if it sounds like the kind of performance Day 4 has been gently dismantling — notice the verse is not a burden you are taking on. It is a sentence you are carrying because the sentence is good. The verse says the gospel is power and the response is trust. There is no homework here. There is only a small thing to keep in your pocket.

modules.heading: Coming Honestly
modules.body:
Luther's letter and Rachel's Tuesday on the floor of her Pittsburgh apartment are saying the same thing in different vocabularies. The medieval theologian's Latin and the modern architect's silence both point at the same reality. The work is finished. The only response left is to come honestly.

What does that look like, in practice, in the next twenty-four hours?

It does not look like a new program. The whole point of these two readings is that the program model is what was wrong. If Day 4 sends you out to do another spiritual project — a thirty-day plan, a new prayer technique, a fresh discipline — Day 4 has missed itself. The right response to receiving a finished work is not to start a new construction project on top of it.

It looks like coming closer, with what is actually in you, to the person whose work this is.

Tim Keller, the New York pastor who died in 2023, wrote a book on marriage in 2011. Tucked inside it is one of the cleanest modern sentences ever written about why being honestly known is so frightening to most of us:

'To be loved but not known is comforting but superficial. To be known and not loved is our greatest fear. But to be fully known and truly loved is, well, a lot like being loved by God.'

Keller is talking about marriage in the chapter the sentence sits in, but the structural claim is theological. There are two failure modes in our experience of being known by another person. One is the comfort of being loved by someone who does not actually know us — a love that floats on a curated version of the self. The other is the terror of being known by someone who, having seen us, has stopped loving us. Most human relationships involve some shifting compromise between those two. We let people see only what we trust them to love. We hide the rest. We accept a thinner intimacy because the alternative — being seen and rejected — is worse.

What the gospel announces is that those two failure modes are not the only options. There is a third. To be fully known and, having been fully known, truly loved. Keller's claim is that this is what relationship with the God of the four-line creed actually is.

For the reader who has been performing — for Rachel and for everyone like Rachel — this is the news of the gospel translated into the only language the heart actually speaks. You do not need to clean up first. You do not need to come with the imaginary, sanitized version of yourself. You can come known. You will not be turned away. The robe is already on the chair.

What does coming honestly look like in the body? It looks like saying out loud, in a quiet room, the thing about yourself you have been trying not to say. It looks like writing the sentence down on a piece of paper and reading it once. It looks like sitting in silence with something you have been keeping in motion for years. It looks like, possibly, weeping for a few minutes about the climbing you have been doing and the energy you have spent trying to build a scaffolding the gospel was already standing in front of.

It does not look, in any of these cases, like a sinner's prayer. The Bible is unhurried about the moment of conversion. It almost never presses people. Jesus, in the gospels, lets the rich young ruler walk away. He lets Nicodemus come back at night a second time. He does not chase the woman at the well with a closing argument; he sends her back into her town and lets the news find its own way through her. The God of the four-line creed has time. The pressure to perform a fast decision is not coming from Him.

What coming honestly does require is the willingness to stop performing. It is harder than it sounds, especially for a reader who has performed for a long time. The hand has learned to clench. Letting it open is a small, real act of courage.

This is also why the Reformers spoke of faith as a gift. Pistis, emunah — the trust the gospel calls for is not, strictly speaking, something the human being manufactures and then offers. It is something that arrives when the human being stops manufacturing. It rises in the open hand the moment the open hand is honest.

If, reading this paragraph, you notice in yourself a small wish that what is being described might be true — a small willingness to come closer with the un-tidied version of yourself — that wish is not nothing. That wish is something arriving from outside you, the way warm air arrives in a room when a window opens. Receive it. You do not have to know what it is yet.

Faith from start to finish.

modules.prompt: Where, in your own history with religion or spirituality, did you start to confuse the climbing for the doorway? What were you trying to perform, and for whom?
additionalQuestions: Of Keller's three categories — loved but not known, known but not loved, fully known and truly loved — which one most accurately describes how you have experienced God up to now?
If the work in the four-line creed really is finished — if the verb is past tense and the response is trust — what is one performance you could lay down today without anyone noticing but you?
If you were writing Luther's letter to a younger version of yourself, what is the one sentence you would underline?

modules.heading: The Open Hand at Day's Close
modules.body:
We started this day with a word you may have inherited without choosing — the word faith — and the modern English shape it has slumped into. We close with the older muscle of that word, the one that has lived in three languages and survived two thousand years of use.

Faith is trust. Trust is the posture of a person whose hand is open. The open hand is the hand of someone who has come honestly to a finished work, and the finished work is what the four lines from yesterday described. The runner who reached the gate of your city carries news that is past tense. The verbs were done before the runner left the battlefield. Your job, reading the news, is not to win the battle. The battle was already won. Your job is, simply, to receive that it was won, and to walk forward as a person inside the news.

If this is the first time you have heard faith described this way, sit with it for a minute before you go anywhere with it. The word has had a lot of work done on it by your culture, your history, possibly a church or two along the way. The original muscle takes a moment to come back.

For the reader who has tried for years to be a good Christian and noticed the trying was the obstacle, the news of this day is the same news Luther was writing to Melanchthon at midnight. You do not need to bring the imaginary, sanitized version of yourself. You can bring the real one. The God of the four-line creed has time, and the work is already done.

For the reader who came here carrying religious harm, what was done to you in the name of God did not match the four lines and did not match the letter from the tower of Wartburg. Whatever was demanded of you in performance was not the gospel. The gospel was not for sale and was never asking for the things that were asked of you. If part of what is happening on this page is a small thawing of that — a small willingness to consider the thing itself might be different from the thing you were given — that thawing is not a betrayal of your honest experience. It is, possibly, your honest experience finding its way to the actual news.

Tomorrow we close the loop.

There is a story in the book of Acts about a man on a desert road, traveling home from Jerusalem in a chariot, reading the prophet Isaiah. He does not know what he is reading. He does not know what he is looking for. He only knows something is moving in him, that the words on the scroll are reaching for something inside him he cannot yet name. A stranger climbs into the chariot beside him, and the stranger explains the words. The man, looking up from the scroll, sees water by the side of the road. He says, almost in passing: what is to prevent me?

That sentence is where the series ends. Not in a decision. Not in a creed. In a man on a road, reading scripture, finding what he had not known he was looking for, and asking what is in his way.

For today, hold this. The hand opens. The work is done. The runner has reached the gate. And the news he is carrying is, in the deepest possible sense, news for tired people first.

modules.title: A Prayer for the Hand That Has Been Trying
modules.prayerText:
Jesus, I have been clenching for a long time.

I did not always know I was clenching. I thought I was being faithful. I thought I was doing what I was supposed to do. I thought the trying was what You wanted from me.

If Luther's letter is true, and Paul's verse is true, and the four lines are true, then the trying was never what You were asking for. The trust was. I do not know how to do that yet, exactly, but I am willing to find out.

I bring You the unsanitized version of myself today. The actual one. The one I have not been showing the people in my life. The one I have not always wanted to show myself.

I cannot promise that my hand will stay open. I have spent too long teaching it to clench. I can only promise that, for this minute, I am willing to let it be open. If You are who You said You were — if the work is finished, if the righteousness is given rather than demanded — please come closer. Please be patient with the parts of me that do not yet know how to receive.

Faith from start to finish, You said. I am at the start. Meet me here.

Amen.

modules.title: The Hand of the Fourth Day
modules.commitment: Today I will let one performance fall away. Whatever I have been doing to make myself acceptable — the verse, the prayer, the program, the careful interior tidying — I will set it down for one day and come honestly. Faith from start to finish. Empty hands.
leavingAtCross: The inherited definition of faith as private belief held without evidence.
The clenched-fist posture of the hand that has been trying to earn what was already given.
The imaginary, sanitized version of myself I have been bringing instead of the actual one.
The assumption that the cleaning-up has to happen before the approach.
receivingFromCross: Faith as trust — pistis and emunah — as the posture of a whole life leaning on a person.
Permission to come with the real version of myself, not the presentable one.
The verb tense of the gospel — finished, past, done — as the ground I stand on rather than the standard I have to clear.
Romans 1:16 as a sentence I can carry in my pocket for the rest of the week.
modules.content: Today I will let one performance fall away. Whatever I have been doing to make myself acceptable — the verse, the prayer, the program, the careful interior tidying — I will set it down for one day and come honestly. Faith from start to finish. Empty hands.

modules.title: Sources for Today's Reading
modules.intro: The two voices quoted today, with full citations.

resources.title: Martin Luther, Letter to Philip Melanchthon (August 1, 1521)
resources.author: Martin Luther
resources.citation: Martin Luther, Letter to Philip Melanchthon, August 1, 1521, in Luther's Works, vol. 48: Letters I, ed. and trans. Gottfried G. Krodel, Fortress Press, 1963, pp. 281-282.
resources.quote: God does not save those who are only imaginary sinners. Be a sinner, and let your sins be strong, but let your trust in Christ be stronger.
resources.context: Written from Wartburg Castle in hiding after the Diet of Worms. The Latin original is esto peccator et pecca fortiter, sed fortius fide et gaude in Christo — be a sinner and sin strongly, but trust more strongly and rejoice in Christ.

resources.title: Tim Keller, The Meaning of Marriage (2011)
resources.author: Timothy Keller
resources.citation: Timothy Keller with Kathy Keller, The Meaning of Marriage: Facing the Complexities of Commitment with the Wisdom of God, Dutton (Penguin Group), New York, 2011, p. 95.
resources.quote: To be loved but not known is comforting but superficial. To be known and not loved is our greatest fear. But to be fully known and truly loved is, well, a lot like being loved by God.
resources.context: Keller, a pastor in Manhattan from 1989 until 2017. The three-part frame — loved but not known, known but not loved, fully known and truly loved — is one of the cleanest contemporary expressions of the gospel's offer.

resources.title: Romans 1:16-17 (Berean Standard Bible)
resources.context: The verse Luther traced his theological breakthrough to. His 1545 autobiographical preface describes the moment 'the righteousness of God' shifted in his reading from a standard he had to meet to a gift he received.

resources.title: Habakkuk 2:4 (King James Version)
resources.context: Paul quotes this verse in Romans 1:17. The Hebrew word translated 'faith' is emunah — from a root meaning to support, to be firm, to carry. KJV chosen for the literary echo into Romans.
